keep: The idea is named up front: readings often pile into a bell, so counting SDs from the mean shows how unusual a reading is.

The picture is the brief's bell and ruler (dataviz lesson 3): an example UPS output on rounds, 115.0 V with 0.3 V of random error read to 0.1 V, the same ratios as the prototype's 27.00 V, 0.03 V and 0.01 V, so its seed and its limits (here 114.2 and 115.8 V) carry over. Skyline to bell, bands counted, limits growing, a reading out shivering, the 'Batches with a reading out' tally and the ringed bead dragged along the SD ruler.

Worked numbers computed from shown rules: 68% of 50 is 34, 5% of 50 is 2.5, half of 5% is one time in forty, (116.0 − 115.0) ÷ 0.3 ≈ 3.3, 1.2 ÷ 0.3 = 4, 0.8 ÷ 0.3 ≈ 2.7, the practice example's 3.7 SD and its 0.3 SD retest.

Each brief misconception has a DO with its own hint: the rule as a formula (screen 4 counts it on fifty beads), deleting the awkward reading (screen 10), one honest reading out read as a fault (screen 8), the rule used on a leaning pile (screen 13).
Thirteen screens alternate SHOW (1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11) and DO (2, 4, 6, 8, 10), ending with two mixed puzzles (12, 13).

Three footnotes, one per sentence, on figures he might look up: 95% within 2 SD, 99.7% within 3 SD with the 3.3 SD convention, and 'ask why before rejecting'. No source named in the text. The 3.3 is called a convention.

Analogy from his trade: a supply quoted as a percentage high, so 115 V and 440 V systems compare, with where it breaks (a chosen rating against the readings' own scatter; the shares come from the bell).
fix: Unsourced claim stated bare: 'Real repeat readings often pile into a similar bell' and 'Textbooks give about 68%'. Put both as 'textbooks add that', the prompt's form for a standard fact with no quote.
False absolute: 'the share ... is the same for every bell' and the analogy's 'equally unusual on any bell'. True only of a normal curve, not of every bell-shaped pile. Say 'every normal curve'.
Causal step skipped: why the ruler is measured from the other forty-nine readings. Say a far-out reading pulls the mean towards it and widens the SD, which shrinks its own count of SDs.
Causal step skipped on screen 12: why the 5% beyond 2 SD splits evenly. Say the bell is symmetric.
Screen 4's wrong pick 'about 15' is not computed from anything. Make it about 16, the 32% of 50 beyond 1 SD, the slip a reader really makes.
'a slip, a loose lead or a real change' lists a loose lead beside a slip as if different. Say 'a slip, such as a loose lead, or a real change'.
